mappings.note: Definition of power of accommodation - the lens changing focal length. LO-4's accommodation clause exactly; no defect is named so LO-5 does not apply.
Near point and far point of a NORMAL eye are the limits of healthy accommodation, so LO-4. LO-5 would be right only if a defect had shifted them.

Cannot read the board from the last row = far vision failing = myopia, and the item also asks for the correction. LO-5 covers naming the defect and selecting the lens; LO-4 covers only the normal eye.
Distractors are defect names but the keyed answer is accommodation, so the outcome tested is LO-4. Stored concept tag 'Presbyopia' is wrong.
Names the part of the eye where the image forms (retina) - the structure clause of LO-4, not accommodation and not a defect.
Numerical value of the least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye; a property of the normal eye's near point, so LO-4 rather than the defect outcome LO-5.
Ciliary muscles change the focal length - the mechanism of accommodation named in LO-4.
Far point at 150 cm identifies myopia and the item asks for the nature (concave) and power of the correcting lens - LO-5's 'selects the type of lens that corrects each'.
Named defect hypermetropia, its correction diagram and the power of the convex lens. LO-5, not LO-4, because the near point has been displaced by a defect.
Why a NORMAL eye cannot focus nearer than 25 cm - the limit of accommodation, LO-4. No defect is present so LO-5 is false here.
Image distance is fixed at the retina while the lens accommodates - directly LO-4's accommodation clause.
Twinkling of stars is the worked example named inside C 5.3-LO-2; it is atmospheric refraction, not scattering (C 8.1-LO-4).
Planets as extended sources whose point-to-point fluctuations average out - the same atmospheric-refraction outcome as twinkling, LO-2 of C 5.3.
Reddening of the sun near the horizon is the second example named in C 8.1-LO-4. Atmospheric refraction (C 5.3-LO-2) explains the sun's early appearance, not its colour.
Dark sky for an astronaut is the absence of scattering - the blue-sky half of C 8.1-LO-4 argued in reverse.
Naming the angles on a prism ray diagram - the ray-diagram apparatus of C 8.1-LO-3. Figure-dependent item.
Identifying incident, refracted and emergent rays on the prism diagram; the prism ray diagram belongs to C 8.1-LO-3, not to the eye or to scattering.
Same prism ray diagram, different labels. C 8.1-LO-3 because the whole item is the geometry of refraction through a prism.
Requires the VIBGYOR order in the dispersed spectrum; the everyday colours are only cues to positions. Dispersion (LO-3), not scattering (LO-4), even though the sky is mentioned.
Range restricted at both ends (50-300 cm) - presbyopia needing bifocals. LO-5 names presbyopia and the corrective lens; LO-4 covers only the unimpaired range.
Blurred board from the LAST desk, clear from the front = myopia; item asks for defect ray diagrams and the concave lens. Stored concept tag 'Rainbow Formation' is wrong.
Mirror image of the previous item - blurred from the FRONT desk = hypermetropia, corrected by a convex lens. Stored concept tag 'Rainbow Formation' is wrong.
Far point pulled in to 10 m names myopia and asks for the correction diagram - LO-5. LO-4 would apply only if the far point were normal.
Cannot see the board at 5 m = myopia; asks defect, correction diagram, lens type and two causes, all of which sit in LO-5. Stored concept tag 'Planets Do Not Twinkle' is wrong.

Judging whether positions 3 and 5 hold the sky's blue and the yolk's yellow tests the ORDER of the dispersed spectrum, so LO-3. Stored concept tag 'Blue Colour of Sky' points at scattering and is wrong.
Prism disperses, a slab does not, because a slab's faces are parallel - the prism geometry inside C 8.1-LO-3.
Far point at 2 m gives a -0.5 D concave lens; selecting the correcting lens is LO-5's own clause. Stored concept tag 'Power of Accommodation' is wrong - no accommodation is computed.
Distance vision intact but near vision lost means the NEAR point has receded - the defining shift of hypermetropia, so LO-5. LO-4 covers the normal near point, which this eye no longer has.
Choosing the prism orientation that puts blue third from the top is a question about the spectrum produced by dispersion - C 8.1-LO-3.
The noon sun is white because the short overhead path scatters least - the scattering outcome LO-4, the same mechanism as the red setting sun.
Lists refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in a raindrop - the rainbow clause of C 8.1-LO-3. Scattering plays no part in a rainbow, so LO-4 is false.
Explicitly attributes twinkling to refraction by layers of varying refractive index - atmospheric refraction, C 5.3-LO-2, and the distractors are there to separate it from scattering and dispersion.
Blue sky from preferential scattering of short wavelengths - the first named example in C 8.1-LO-4.
All colours travel at the same speed in air but not in glass - the reason dispersion happens in a prism at all, so LO-3 rather than the scattering outcome.
Red is chosen for danger signals because it is scattered least by smoke and fog - a scattering application, C 8.1-LO-4, not dispersion.
MCQ that pits scattering against dispersion and total internal reflection for the red sunrise; the keyed answer is scattering, C 8.1-LO-4.
The blue of deep sea traces back to the scattering that makes the sky blue; C 8.1-LO-4 is the only outcome covering colour produced by scattering.
Most refraction happens at the outer surface of the cornea - a fact about the structure of the eye, LO-4. Stored concept tag 'Scattering of Light' is wrong.
Relaxed ciliary muscles, thinner lens, longer focal length - the accommodation mechanism of LO-4, tested on a healthy eye.
Asks which statement about myopia and hypermetropia is true; it is a straight discrimination between the two defects, LO-5.
Ray diagrams of the myopic and hypermetropic EYE - defect diagrams, LO-5. Stored concept tag 'Human Eye Structure' points at LO-4, which covers only the normal eye.
Advice to a student who cannot read the board from the back plus the correction diagram - identify myopia and select the concave lens, LO-5.
How a normal eye handles near and far objects is accommodation, LO-4; no defect is implied, so LO-5 would be false.
A -4.5 D prescription identifies myopia and a concave lens; naming the defect from the lens power is LO-5's selection clause read backwards.
Newton's second prism recombining the spectrum into white light - dispersion through a prism, C 8.1-LO-3. Stem carries mojibake ('secÂ¬ond').
The apparent position of a star is raised by atmospheric refraction - the same bending that gives advanced sunrise in C 5.3-LO-2.
Rainbow needs suspended water drops to refract, disperse and internally reflect sunlight - the rainbow clause of C 8.1-LO-3.
Blue sky by scattering - C 8.1-LO-4 names this example explicitly.

Colour of the sun at sunrise/sunset versus noon is decided by path length through the atmosphere and hence by scattering, LO-4. Stored concept tag 'Advance Sunrise & Delayed Sunset' points at refraction and is wrong - nothing here is about timing.
Naming the cornea - the structure clause of LO-4.
Function of the iris in regulating light entering the eye - part structure and function, LO-4, not lens accommodation and not a defect.
Function of the pupil; a structure-and-function recall covered by LO-4.
Naming the iris from its description as a muscular diaphragm - LO-4's structure clause.
The eye lens is convex; a structural fact about the eye, LO-4.
Names the ciliary muscles as the agent of accommodation - LO-4's accommodation clause.
Names accommodation itself; LO-4 is the only outcome that defines it.
Real and inverted image on the retina - how the normal eye forms its image, LO-4.
Retina as the screen of the eye - structure clause of LO-4.
Value of the near point for a normal eye, a limit of normal accommodation, so LO-4 and not the defect outcome.
Value of the far point (infinity) for a normal eye - same normal-accommodation limit, LO-4.
